subtype: Approach: adjusting study and exam plans with school support [Action]
passage:
Devika: how did it go with Mrs Rao?
Shalini: I told her about Nani. Just said it flat, then cried in the corridor
Devika: oh Shali. what did she say
Shalini: that I don't have to perform normal right now. Extra time on the two assignments, four weeks
Devika: that's good?
Shalini: I think so. I wasn't sleeping and I kept staring at the page
Shalini: we made a lighter plan. One subject a night, weekends free
Devika: want me to sit with you at lunch?
Shalini: yes please
Shalini: it felt like putting a bag down. I'm still sad but I can breathe a bit
Devika: I'm here

qa.q: How long is the extra time on the two assignments?
qa.a: The extra time on the two assignments is four weeks.

qa.q: How does Shalini feel after the talk with Mrs Rao?
qa.a: Shalini feels some relief, as if putting a heavy bag down, though still sad.

qa.q: What else could support Shalini besides the lighter plan?
qa.a: Shalini could talk to the school counsellor and keep friends close, since a lighter plan eases the work but not the grief itself.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao see Shalini's request?
qa.a: Mrs Rao seems understanding, since she tells Shalini there is no need to perform normal right now.

grounding: A teen tells the class teacher about a bereavement, asks for extra time on assignments for a few weeks and builds a lighter schedule.

subtype: Approach: adjusting study and exam plans with school support [Action]
passage: Two weeks after his Amma's sudden death, Jagdish still couldn't finish a single page of homework. The fields needed him before school, his little sister needed him after, and at night the house was too quiet to think. On Monday he waited behind after class at the government high school in Hosakote. "Sangeeta Madam, I can't keep up right now." She put down her chalk and listened. Together they looked at what was due: a science project, two maths worksheets, the Kannada essay. "The essay can wait three weeks," she said. "Do one maths sheet this week, not two. I'll speak to the science teacher." Jagdish wrote a new plan in his notebook: one subject a night, forty minutes, then sleep. The first week, he finished everything on it. It wasn't much, but it was done.

qa.a: A science project, two maths worksheets and the Kannada essay.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when he waited behind after class?
qa.a: Jagdish felt overwhelmed and worn out, grieving his Amma while the fields and his sister filled his days.

qa.q: What else could help Jagdish once the three weeks are over?
qa.a: He could meet Sangeeta Madam again to review the plan and add work back slowly, rather than jumping straight to a full load.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta Madam see Jagdish's request?
qa.a: She sees a grieving student who is trying, so she lightens the load and speaks to the science teacher instead of expecting normal work at once.

grounding: Shows a teen telling the class teacher after his mother's death, getting extra time on some work and building a lighter study plan.

subtype: Approach: adjusting study and exam plans with school support [Action]
passage: Bao's grandmother died of a stroke on a Thursday, three weeks before the mid-year exams. She had lived with them in the flat above the bakery in Footscray and walked Bao to school for nine years. By the next Tuesday, Bao had read the same history chapter five times without remembering a line. At lunch, Priscila watched Bao stare at an untouched sandwich. "You should tell Mr. Hale." "Everyone's got exams." "Everyone's grandmother didn't just die." That afternoon Bao went to the homeroom teacher's desk. Mr. Hale listened, then pulled up the calendar. They moved the history essay and the science report back three weeks. Bao crossed out the old study timetable and made a smaller one: an hour a day, one subject, Sundays off. It felt like cheating at first. By Friday, it felt like breathing.

qa.q: How many times had Bao read the history chapter?
qa.a: Bao had read the same history chapter five times.

qa.q: Why did Bao at first resist telling Mr. Hale?
qa.a: Bao felt guilty about asking for special treatment when everyone had exams, even while too grief-struck to study.

qa.q: What else could help Bao as the exams come closer?
qa.a: Bao could check in with Mr. Hale each week and add more study only when the smaller timetable feels steady.

qa.q: How does Priscila see what Bao is going through?
qa.a: Priscila notices the untouched sandwich and understands this is more than exam stress, so Priscila pushes gently for Bao to get help.

grounding: Illustrates a teen telling the teacher after a grandmother's sudden death, getting deadlines moved and making a lighter timetable instead of forcing normal work.
